certainty_reasoning: Against the README bar - that the desire be legible as desire to a reader who does not already hold the coding hypothesis - this project reads this as clearing it, on the strength of the four-sentence run itself: a named young man, a physical description ('He has fair hair, and is always in dark blue'), the fact that Wilde has written ahead to arrange the meeting ('I have written to him'), and then, immediately, an explicit statement of longing set against virginity - 'After the chill virginity of Swiss Alps and snow, I long for the red flowers of life that stain the feet of summer in Italy.' A reader without the hypothesis reads an older man looking forward to a young man he has written to. What such a reader would not independently supply is the sexual character, and that is not proposed here. Whose reading: the agent's, as transcriber; no scholarly source was consulted, and the editors' index classing 'Rolla, Edoardo (boy)' (triage mirror, unverified in the source) is an editorial classing, not a reading of desire. Outcome is genuinely unknown rather than unreciprocated: nothing in the pages read says whether the meeting happened. COOLING DOCUMENTED 2026-08-05: printed 1141, read at the page, has Wilde telling Smithers 'I do not love the lad Edoardo Rolla as much as I did' - within weeks of the Genoa meeting. It does not change the class; it bounds the duration.
date_label: Anticipated meeting at Genoa, first week of April 1899. The letter is dated '[early April 1899]' by the editors; the two Ross postcards on the same printed page are postmarked 7 April 1899 from Santa Margherita.
summary: Leaving Mellor's villa at Gland at the start of April 1899, Wilde wrote to Robert Ross that he hoped to find a young seaman named Edoardo Rolla waiting for him at Genoa, having written ahead to him, and set the hope beside a statement of longing for Italy after the Swiss months. It is an approach on the page and nothing more: no letter read records whether the two met, and Rolla appears nowhere else in the correspondence consulted.

sources.quote: I hope to find at Genoa, waiting for me, a young lad, by name Edoardo Rolla, one of the sea-farers. He has fair hair, and is always in dark blue. I have written to him. After the chill virginity of Swiss Alps and snow, I long for the red flowers of life that stain the feet of summer in Italy. Ever yours O. W.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, [early April 1899], Gland - the final paragraph of the letter announcing his departure for Genoa, where he had taken a room at the Albergo di Firenze on the quay.
sources.supports: The approach itself: a named young man written to in advance, described, and awaited, with Wilde's longing stated in the same breath; no outcome recorded
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1186, printed folio 1140 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: My dear Smithers, … The £10 arrived safe - many thanks. Of course it was a blow not getting the £20, but I do hope you will send the balance soon. I now want to get back to Paris - my life here is too lonely. … Is there really any chance of your coming out here? I wish you would. I am at Santa Margherita, Ligure, Genoa, where please write and send the DC: the only consolation I have as I do not love the lad Edoardo Rolla as much as I did. Yours
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [? 8 April 1899], Albergo di Firenze, Genoa (MS Simpson). The elisions drop the proofs of the play and a request for £100. THE END OF IT, in the same sentence as an address for forwarding: the Daily Chronicle is to be sent on because Rolla is no longer consolation enough. Wilde had met him at Genoa that same April, so this is a matter of weeks. Nothing is said about what Rolla felt, then or now.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That the attachment cooled, and how fast - stated by Wilde himself to a third party.
